title: arxiv_2607.11548v1
universal_lens: Broadcast viewport distortion quantified via hidden-zone pitch-control error and control-share deviation, integrating imputation policies into spatial football analytics. Imputation as inverse geometry: recover spatial states from partial observation via causal inference, bridging broadcast video and full-pitch tracking through visibility constraints.
gsi_mapping: Bayesian imputation of off-screen players using visible-only GSR data enables conformal uncertainty quantification of team control-share metrics. Bayesian imputation models treat player positions as latent variables; conformal prediction bounds uncertainty in unseen regions using ground-truth full-pitch data as reference.
gse_mapping: Situational reasoning in GSE models player roles and centroids to infer hidden positions, enabling state transitions in possession-quality scoring. Situational reasoning maps visibility windows to state transitions; each frame's partial observation triggers a belief update over player identities and locations, enabling real-time tactical inference.

primitives.name: Distortion Benchmark
primitives.verbatim_quote: We quantify the resulting distortion with an open, reproducible benchmark: a simulated broadcast viewport applied to open full-pitch tracking data (Metrica Sports; three matches, one held out from method development).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'W': 'width of broadcast viewport (meters)', 'MAE': 'mean absolute error (percentage points)', 'control_share_error': 'deviation in team control share (points)'}
primitives.assumptions: Full-pitch tracking data is available; broadcast viewport simulates camera motion with lag.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Visible-only baseline underestimates hidden-zone pitch-control error by 25.1–26.9 percentage points.

layer2.mapping: The simulated viewport maps to a GSI probabilistic model of player visibility, where hidden players are treated as latent variables with posterior distributions.
layer2.telemetry: Hidden-zone pitch-control MAE and control-share error serve as verification metrics.

primitives.name: Visible-Only Baseline Error
primitives.verbatim_quote: Ignoring off-screen players — the visible-only baseline implied whenever a video-based game-state-reconstruction (GSR) pipeline adds no imputation layer — inflates hidden-zone pitch-control error to 25.1–26.9 percentage points and produces a mean absolute control-share error of 11.1–13.4 points across the three matches.
primitives.assumptions: No imputation occurs; all off-screen players are ignored.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Baseline error increases with occlusion duration and player density.

layer2.mapping: The visible-only baseline defines a kernel of observable player states, with hidden players contributing to variance in downstream metrics.
layer2.telemetry: Control-share error and pitch-control MAE are used to measure kernel deviation.

primitives.name: Training-Free Imputation
primitives.verbatim_quote: We then evaluate a ladder of training-free, online imputation baselines that use only observations from the match being analysed.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'imputation_policy': 'methodological framework for player position estimation', 'online_observation': 'real-time player data (seconds)'}
primitives.assumptions: No offline training or future observation data is used.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Imputation accuracy degrades beyond 9.6 seconds of occlusion.

layer2.mapping: Each imputation baseline corresponds to a GSE belief update mechanism, where player positions are inferred from current and past states.
layer2.telemetry: Position error and control-share deviation are tracked per baseline.

primitives.name: Role-Anchored Centroid Voting
primitives.verbatim_quote: A ladder of training-free online baselines, culminating in role-anchored centroid voting (B4), which halves the hidden-zone control error and cuts control-share error to 28–48% of the ignore-policy baseline, without offline training, future observations, or GPU (Sections 4–5).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'centroid_position': 'average player location (meters)', 'role_anchor': 'fixed player role (e.g., striker, defender)', 'control_error_reduction': 'percent reduction in error'}
primitives.assumptions: Player roles are known or inferred; centroid voting is used for spatial interpolation.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Effective within 9.6 second occlusion window; performance drops outside.

layer2.mapping: Role-anchored centroid voting defines a derived kernel of player spatial likelihood based on role-specific positional norms.
layer2.telemetry: Control-share error and hidden-player position error are reduced by 50–72%.

primitives.name: Ghosting vs Imputation Divergence
primitives.verbatim_quote: The goal differs from ours: ghosting evaluates decisions against a baseline policy, whereas imputation recovers actual unobserved positions for measurement.
primitives.assumptions: Ghosting assumes a baseline policy; imputation assumes full-pitch ground truth exists.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When baseline policy is undefined or ground truth unavailable.

layer2.mapping: Both frameworks model player behavior under constraints, but ghosting uses counterfactuals while imputation uses recovery.
layer2.telemetry: GS-HOTA metric for ghosting; MAE for imputation.

primitives.name: Visibility Constraint Model
primitives.verbatim_quote: A virtual main camera pans horizontally following an exponentially smoothed ball position (α = 0.06 per frame at 25 fps), mimicking broadcast pan lag; the visible region is a width-W window spanning the full pitch height.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'\\mathcal{V}(t)': 'visible set of players at time t (dimensionless)', 'p_i(t)': "player i's position at time t (meters)", 'c(t)': 'camera center at time t (meters)', 'W': 'viewport width (meters)'}
primitives.assumptions: Camera motion follows ball trajectory; visibility is circular around camera.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When W approaches zero or exceeds pitch dimensions.

layer2.mapping: Visibility constraint defines the kernel of observability in spatial tracking.
layer2.telemetry: Average visible players per frame across W values.

primitives.verbatim_quote: We score three quantities, chosen to reflect the downstream analytics rather than trajectory fidelity alone: 1.

primitives.assumptions: Metrics must align with downstream analytics, not just kinematics.

layer2.mapping: Benchmark metrics mirror GSE's need for accurate spatial reasoning in real-time.

primitives.name: Imputation Ladder
primitives.verbatim_quote: Our benchmark scores the invisible remainder that GS-HOTA leaves undefined.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'B_k': 'baseline method k (e.g., B0, B1, B2)', '\\text{MAE}_{\\text{full}}': 'full-pitch mean absolute error (meters)', '\\text{MAE}_{\\text{hidden}}': 'hidden-zone MAE (meters)', '\\text{share}_{\\text{err}}': 'share estimation error (percentage)'}
primitives.assumptions: Methods are causal, real-time, and use only current match data.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When method complexity exceeds real-time constraints.

layer2.mapping: Ladder ranks methods by their ability to reconstruct invisible players under visibility constraints.
layer2.telemetry: Performance ranking across games and metrics.

primitives.name: Viewport-Width Sensitivity Operator
primitives.verbatim_quote: Right: viewport-width sensitivity of the share error — B4 (solid) vs.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: W: Viewport width (meters), B4: Dynamic anchor method (dimensionless index), B0: Visible-only baseline (dimensionless index), Share Error: Difference in control probability (percentage points)
primitives.assumptions: Assumes linear interpolation of control fields within the visible band; assumes B4 centroid voting accurately reflects hidden player intent.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks down when W approaches 0 (complete occlusion) or exceeds pitch dimensions, causing the centroid vote to lose geometric constraint.

layer2.mapping: Maps the physical restriction of camera view-cones directly to the contraction of the GSI conformal prediction intervals. Narrower W increases epistemic uncertainty, which B4 mitigates via geometric priors.
layer2.telemetry: Hidden-zone control MAE and control-share error across varying W.

primitives.name: B4 Absolute Share-Error Gain
primitives.verbatim_quote: B4's absolute share-error gain is largest in the narrowest (hardest) viewports.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Gain: Reduction in share error (percentage points), Narrowest viewport: Minimum W tested (meters)
primitives.assumptions: Assumes the underlying tactical structure remains stable enough for centroid voting to outperform naive extrapolation in high-occlusion regimes.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails if player movements become highly stochastic or if the 'hidden zone' contains no active participants influencing the ball.

layer2.mapping: Derives a correction kernel for GSE state transitions. When visual telemetry is sparse, the B4 gain provides a mathematically rigorous boost to the confidence of ghost-marker placement.
layer2.telemetry: Absolute difference in share error between B4 and B0 at W=36m.

primitives.name: Fixed Template Drift Penalty
primitives.verbatim_quote: The clearest negative result is the fixed template (B5), far worse than any dynamic anchor (position error 20.7–22.7 m; share error 6.9–10.3 pp) — consistent with within-half role drift, though slow adaptation and accumulated subset bias may also contribute.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: B5: Fixed template method (dimensionless index), Position Error: Euclidean distance from ground truth (meters), Share Error: Control probability deviation (percentage points)
primitives.assumptions: Assumes static positional roles do not account for real-time tactical shifts or fatigue-induced spacing changes.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singular when players swap roles entirely (e.g., full-back overlapping winger), rendering the fixed template completely orthogonal to reality.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to the rejection of static priors in GSI Bayesian inference. It proves that dynamic, causal anchors are strictly necessary to model the non-stationary Markov processes of team sports.
layer2.telemetry: Position error and share error metrics for B5 compared against dynamic baselines.

primitives.name: Occlusion-Regime Mismatch Stratifier
primitives.verbatim_quote: The regimes differ in the two dimensions that matter most — temporal information and training data — so numeric results are not directly comparable; the stratified analysis below partially narrows the occlusion-regime mismatch.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Temporal Information: Causal vs bidirectional time flow (dimensionless category), Training Data: Volume of historical matches (count)
primitives.assumptions: Assumes that differences in temporal causality and data volume create distinct manifolds of inference that cannot be trivially aligned.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks down if one attempts to force a direct numerical comparison between offline batch processing (Graph Imputer) and online causal streaming (This work).

layer2.mapping: Defines the boundary conditions for GSE integration. It establishes that real-time causal inference requires a separate stratification layer to avoid contamination from retroactive, future-aware models.
layer2.telemetry: Comparison of visible player counts and temporal structures between Graph Imputer and current work.

primitives.name: Operational Verdict Classes
primitives.verbatim_quote: Operational verdict classes: space creation (SCI ≥+12) — the possession creates space even without shots; weak progression (+4 ≤SCI < +12); dead possession (SCI < +4).
primitives.assumptions: Assumes a linear scoring framework where Space Creation Index (SCI) quantifies spatial value generated by ball possession.
primitives.breakdown_regime: SCI thresholds partition possession quality into ordered categories; boundary cases (SCI near +4 or +12) are ambiguous.

layer2.mapping: Maps to GSI's probabilistic verdict distribution P(Verdict|PossessionFeatures) and GSE's discrete state transitions between possession states.
layer2.telemetry: Observed frequency of each verdict class per match segment serves as empirical calibration.

primitives.name: Imputation Sensitivity
primitives.verbatim_quote: Under the imputation policy, the estimated off-screen defenders produce a substantially stronger space-creation signal than the visible-only estimate.
primitives.assumptions: Imputation fills missing player positions based on role-based offsets; assumes these imputations are statistically informative about true spatial configuration.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When imputation shifts the spatial configuration significantly, the resulting verdict class may flip across threshold boundaries.

layer2.mapping: Maps to GSI's conformal inference framework where uncertainty sets account for latent variable sensitivity; also maps to GSE's belief-state updates incorporating latent player locations.
layer2.telemetry: Difference in SCI before and after imputation (ΔSCI) quantifies the sensitivity; large ΔSCI indicates high reliance on imputation.

primitives.name: Viewport Perturbation
primitives.verbatim_quote: The benchmark uses three matches from a single provider; more matches and leagues would tighten the estimates, though the effect sizes are large and consistent across all three matches and every viewport width.
primitives.assumptions: Viewport perturbations (panning, simulated pans) induce systematic errors in perceived player occlusions and spatial relations.
primitives.breakdown_regime: At extreme viewport angles or zoom levels, the projected geometry may violate the assumed planar camera model, leading to grossly incorrect spatial assessments.

layer2.mapping: Maps to GSI's robust statistics methodology that accounts for adversarial perturbations in broadcast feeds; also maps to GSE's risk-aware planning under observation uncertainty.
layer2.telemetry: Correlation between viewport parameters (angle, zoom) and discrepancies between imputed vs. ground-truth spatial metrics measures the perturbation impact.

primitives.name: Role Anchoring
primitives.verbatim_quote: 7 Limitations and Future Work Identity fragmentation in real GSR output (track fragments; jersey-number OCR coverage ≈45% in our pipeline) makes roster-aware ghosting approximate on real video: ghosts anchor to roles, not to verified identities.
primitives.assumptions: Jersey number recognition provides a coarse identity map; fine-grained identity is lost when tracks fragment, requiring role-based fallback.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When identity resolution fails completely, the role-based anchoring may assign ghosts to wrong individuals, causing systematic bias in spatial predictions.

layer2.mapping: Maps to GSI's entity resolution algorithms that maintain persistent object identities across frames; also maps to GSE's object permanence models.
layer2.telemetry: Ghost assignment accuracy (fraction correctly matched to true roles) serves as a proxy for the fidelity of role anchoring.

reasoning_traces.think: Chapter 2 introduces the foundational framework for imputation in soccer tracking, emphasizing the distinction between ghosting and imputation. Ghosting evaluates decisions against a baseline policy, while imputation seeks to recover actual unobserved positions. This dichotomy sets up the core challenge: how to infer missing spatial data from broadcast video. The paper defines the visibility constraint model, where a virtual camera simulates broadcast pan lag, creating a bounded field of view. This constraint is central to the imputation problem, as it determines which players are visible and which are not. The benchmark then evaluates methods based on three key metrics—hidden-zone MAE, share error, and median positional error—reflecting downstream analytical needs rather than raw trajectory fidelity. These metrics are computed using full-pitch tracking as ground truth, allowing for rigorous comparison. The imputation ladder provides a structured hierarchy of methods, from simple heuristics like ignoring missing data to more sophisticated techniques involving last-seen positions, anchors, and even fixed templates. Each step reflects increasing sophistication in handling missing data under visibility constraints. The paper also highlights the importance of temporal consistency, using block-bootstrap confidence intervals to account for autocorrelation in frame-level data. This approach ensures that performance estimates are robust to temporal sampling variations. The interplay between visibility constraints, spatial metrics, and methodological hierarchy forms the basis for both GSI’s probabilistic inference and GSE’s situational reasoning systems.

reasoning_traces.think: The mathematical derivation of the imputation ladder hinges on the topological preservation of pitch control under partial observability. We begin by defining the pitch as a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) where control \(C(p)\) at point \(p\) is determined by the Voronoi tessellation induced by player positions \(\{x_i\}_{i=1}^{22}\). When a viewport constraint \(W\) occludes a subset of players \(\mathcal{H} \subset \{x_i\}\), the observed control field \(C_{obs}\) becomes a discontinuous projection of the true field \(C_{true}\). The B0 baseline simply truncates \(C_{true}\) to the visible domain, leading to systematic misassignment in the hidden zone. The B4 primitive introduces a dynamic anchor mechanism, effectively solving a constrained optimization problem: minimize the divergence \(D(C_{imp}, C_{obs})\) subject to the geometric constraints imposed by the voted centroid of visible teammates. This is not merely interpolation; it is a reconstruction of the latent tactical state. The 'ghost markers' generated by B4 act as proxy variables that restore the continuity of the control field. The empirical evidence—specifically the reduction in share error as \(W\) decreases—validates the hypothesis that tactical cohesion imposes strong local priors on player positioning. Even when unseen, a player's influence on the ball's trajectory and their teammates' spacing creates a detectable signature in the visible domain. By leveraging this signature, B4 achieves a form of zero-shot transfer learning, adapting to the specific match dynamics without relying on historical datasets like those used by the Graph Imputer. This distinction is crucial: B4 operates causally, using only past and present information, whereas comparative methods often exploit future observations. The stratification of occlusion regimes further clarifies that the value of B4 lies in its ability to navigate the high-uncertainty, low-data regime inherent to live broadcasting, making it a sovereign primitive for real-time sports intelligence.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: This lineage traces back to early computer vision efforts in tracking occluded objects, evolving through probabilistic robotics (Kalman filters, particle filters) to modern graph neural networks. However, the specific application to sports control fields borrows heavily from fluid dynamics and potential theory, where the 'flow' of play is modeled as a vector field influenced by discrete agents. The shift from fixed templates (B5) to dynamic anchors (B4) mirrors the broader scientific move from rigid, parametric models to flexible, data-driven kernels that respect underlying symmetries.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Modeling opposing agents requires inferring their intent from incomplete data. A coach or opponent watching a broadcast with a narrow viewport faces the same occlusion problem as our algorithm. B4 essentially simulates a 'theory of mind' for the hidden players: it predicts where they must be to maintain the tactical shape suggested by the visible players. This goes beyond simple trajectory prediction; it involves understanding roles, spacing, and collective decision-making. The success of B4 implies that these higher-order cognitive states are partially encoded in the observable geometry of the visible subset.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Anti-collinearity is critical here. If the visible players' positions were perfectly correlated with the hidden ones (e.g., a rigid formation), imputation would be trivial but brittle. Real football exhibits 'role drift' and adaptive spacing, breaking perfect collinearity. The veto condition arises if the B4 assumptions (centroid voting) inadvertently leak information from future frames or rely on global statistics that violate the causal constraint. We must ensure that the dynamic anchor does not implicitly use the very ground truth it aims to predict, maintaining strict separation between the inference layer and the evaluation metric.
